transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-12 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Tom (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Luis (Redwood SE), Jamal (CTO Solace), Marta (Head of ML), Omar (Platform), Sofia (Product), Ben (SRE)

Summary: Quick scoping for POC focused on replacing their current OpenAI calls with Redwood's OpenAI-compatible endpoints, evaluating function/tool calling for internal tool orchestration, and validating structured JSON outputs at scale. We covered workload numbers, benchmark plan and timeline.

[00:00:12] Tom (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — can you hear me ok?
[00:00:18] Jamal (Solace): Yep loud and clear, thanks Tom.
[00:00:22] Priya (Redwood): Cool. Quick agenda — run the integration options, confirm workload sizing, define success criteria for the POC and then outline the benchmark plan. Does that look good?
[00:00:30] Marta (Solace): Yep that's perfect. We want to validate performance and that function calling works for our internal tools.
[00:00:36] Tom: Great. Can you give a quick overview of your current infra and how you're calling models today?
[00:00:44] Omar (Solace): Sure — currently we call OpenAI endpoints from a Node backend. We have a gateway that does auth and some caching, but everything is basic. Peak traffic right now is around 180 rps across all services, about 80 concurrent chat sessions. Typical user request is about 1k tokens prompt and 300 tokens returned on average. Monthly usage ~120M tokens.
[00:01:05] Ben (SRE): Also worth noting we need control over egress rules — all outbound calls must originate from our VPC, and we probably will prefer Redwood Private or Dedicated.
[00:01:15] Luis (Redwood): Noted. For the POC, we can run a Dedicated trial so you can validate network constraints and perf. Priya, you wanted to speak on integration patterns?
[00:01:24] Priya: Yeah — two main approaches: 1) point Redwood's OpenAI-compatible endpoint as a drop-in replacement, minimal code change; or 2) use Redwood SDKs (Python/Node) that add streaming helpers, structured output validation and batching helpers. For function calling, we support OpenAI-style function schemas plus Redwood's tool-call hooks for longer-running backend tasks.
[00:01:46] Marta: For us the less friction the better. If it truly is OpenAI-compatible we can just swap endpoints and keep existing function call schemas. We do have a set of tools that expect specific JSON shapes back — the structured output reliability is critical.
[00:01:58] Priya: Totally. We recommend enabling the structured output enforcement mode during the POC — it will return a validation flag alongside the model response and optionally a best-effort repaired JSON if the model deviates. That helps automation.
[00:02:12] Sofia (Product): And about function calling, we need synchronous and async semantics — some tool calls start a long job. How does Redwood handle that?
[00:02:20] Luis: We have a tool-calling flow where function calls can return a call intent with an execution id; Redwood can stream the model intent back, and then your backend can poll or attach a webhook for completion. For the Dedicated run we can show both modes.
[00:02:35] Jamal: Okay that's helpful. Next — success criteria. Marta, what are the must-haves?
[00:02:40] Marta: Accuracy of structured outputs (>= 95% valid JSON for our schema), latency p95 for 300-token responses under 900ms end-to-end, and throughput to support 200 rps sustained (we will test burst to 400 rps). Also memory of the session — KV cache and prefix reuse is important for latency.
[00:03:00] Priya: Good, those are clear. For the latency target, with Redwood Dedicated and a mid-size LLM variant we typically see p95 for 300 tokens around 700–900ms depending on batch settings — we'll tune batching and KV cache settings.
[00:03:12] Omar: Sounds reasonable. Could you clarify token accounting — how do you measure prompt vs generated tokens in the POC?
[00:03:18] Tom: We provide token-level logging in the console and per-request breakdowns in the tracing view, so you'll get prompt vs completion tokens and cost estimates. We'll share an example trace.
[00:03:27] Ben: Any constraints around streaming? We use streaming to update UI progressively.
[00:03:31] Priya: Streaming is supported in both Hosted and Dedicated. For Dedicated we'll show a demo with chunked tokens and a reconnect fallback. Small note — streaming implies more open connections, so we'll account for concurrency in the benchmark.
[00:03:42] Marta: On the topic of concurrency — our current gateway can handle about 1k open sockets but prefer fewer. We'll provide expected concurrent streams.
[00:03:49] Tom: Great. Let's talk exact benchmark plan. Priya?
[00:03:52] Priya: Proposed: a 1-week Dedicated benchmark. Day 0 setup and network validation. Days 1–3 run synthetic load matching your production distribution: 180 rps baseline, bursts to 400 rps; prompt sizes 800–1200 tokens, completion 150–400 tokens. Measure p50/p95/p99 latency, error rates, and structured-output validity. Day 4 run a real prompt set you provide to measure quality regressions. Day 5 analysis and tuning. We'll provide scripts (k6 + custom harness) and share the test runner repo.
[00:04:20] Jamal: That aligns. For success metrics we will require: p95 < 900ms for 300 tokens, structured output >=95% valid, error rate <0.5% over 24h. If those are met we consider this POC successful.
[00:04:33] Luis: Understood. We'll instrument the run and export logs to your S3 for analysis or we can provide CSV exports.
[00:04:40] Omar: Network wise — if we do Dedicated inside Redwood cloud, how do we handle VPC peering / egress? We need private connectivity.
[00:04:48] Tom: For Dedicated we can do a VPC peering option or Private deployment depending on long-term needs. For the week-long benchmark we typically provide a peered subnet and test keys with IP allowlist. We'll share a network checklist.
[00:04:59] Ben: Also KMS — keys must be customer-managed. Is that available for Dedicated?
[00:05:03] Luis: Yes, we integrate with customer KMS for Dedicated/Private. For the POC we'll use encrypted at rest and can show the KMS flow; full BYOK will take a bit longer but we can demo.
[00:05:12] Marta: Quality checks — we want automated evaluation on our prompt set. Do you support eval hooks?
[00:05:18] Priya: We have Redwood Optimize eval harness that can run your test prompts and compare outputs against golden labels, plus regression alerts. For the POC we'll run baseline vs tuned model and produce a quality report.
[00:05:28] Jamal: Excellent. Regarding models, are we using open models or Redwood-curated weights? We need to know the options that meet our latency target.
[00:05:36] Tom: We'll propose a few model variants: 1) smaller low-latency open model for fast responses, 2) medium-sized model for better quality, and 3) quantized variant for cost optimization. Priya will suggest kernel and quantization configs during tuning.
[00:05:50] Sofia: A practical question — if we pointer-swap to Redwood's OpenAI-compatible endpoint, do function calls and tool invocation IDs remain the same shape? Our orchestration expects a certain field.
[00:05:59] Priya: Yes — we maintain compatible schemas for function calling. There may be small name mangles in the transcript export occasionally (auto-transcription issues), but the payload fields for function names, args, and call ids are preserved. We'll send examples.
[00:06:13] Marta: We have some very strict structured outputs (nested JSON with arrays) — how do you handle partial failures where the model returns malformed JSON?
[00:06:20] Luis: That's where structured-output enforcement comes in. The system will either reject the response with an error and a regeneration suggestion, or attempt a best-effort repair and set a validation flag. You can choose strict or lenient mode for the POC.
[00:06:33] Ben: On observability — we need tracing per request and per-token cost breakdown.
[00:06:38] Tom: Console provides per-request traces, latencies, token breakdown, and per-route dashboards. We'll set up a demo tenant with the relevant dashboards during the POC.
[00:06:46] Omar: SLA conversation — for production we'd need uptime numbers. For the POC it's okay but we need to understand transition.
[00:06:52] Tom: We'll include SLA and enterprise contract information in the pricing doc. For Dedicated there are SLA-backed latency/uptime targets.
[00:06:58] Sofia: Timeline — can we start the week of Oct 20 as you proposed?
[00:07:02] Tom: Yes, target start Oct 20. Action items and owners are in the notes.
[00:07:08] Marta: One more thing — we use a legacy internal tool that isn't accessible externally; can we demo function calls to a stubbed endpoint?
[00:07:16] Priya: Absolutely — during the POC we'll use a stub that simulates the long-running job and show both sync and async tool call flows.
[00:07:24] Jamal: Great. Anything else on security/compliance?
[00:07:27] Luis: We'll send SOC2/ISO certs and pen test summaries. For the POC we can supply redacted logs.
[00:07:33] Ben: Fine.
[00:07:36] Tom: Ok let's recap the next steps — I'll send pricing and the Quickstart; Priya will own the benchmark plan and runner; Luis will send security docs; Marta/Omar will provide sample prompts and network constraints. We'll schedule start for Oct 20.
[00:07:51] Marta: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[00:07:54] Tom: Thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the repo links.

(Several short procedural confirmations and chuckles)
